name: Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT)
summary: Nicotine replacement (patch, gum, lozenge, nasal spray) helps you quit smoking by taking the edge off withdrawal—cravings, irritability, restlessness, and that “I can’t think about anything else” feeling—without the thousands of toxic chemicals in cigarettes.
description: NRT gives your brain a controlled, cleaner nicotine “bridge” so quitting doesn’t feel like getting hit by a truck. It won’t magically erase habit and triggers, but it can dramatically reduce cravings, agitation, and withdrawal-driven anxiety. The big rule: you’re quitting smoking—don’t keep smoking on NRT (overdose risk). Best outcomes happen when you pair NRT with a quit plan and behavioral support.
patient_summary: NRT helps you quit by easing nicotine withdrawal (cravings, irritability, restlessness, anxiety-ish agitation). Patch = steady background relief. Gum/lozenge = fast rescue for cravings. Nasal spray = fastest (prescription). Don’t smoke while using NRT—too much nicotine can make you sick. Use it long enough (often 8–12+ weeks) and pair it with a plan.

metadata.prescription_status: OTC (patch/gum/lozenge); Prescription Required (Nicotrol NS nasal spray)

primary_indications: Relief of nicotine withdrawal symptoms (including craving)

linked_conditions.context: NRT is a first-line medication option to support quitting combustible tobacco by reducing withdrawal symptoms that drive relapse.
Targets the withdrawal cluster that often looks psychiatric: irritability, restlessness, agitation, sleep disruption, and concentration problems.
Quitting smoking can wreck sleep early on. Patch can help nighttime withdrawal for some people, but can also cause vivid dreams; some people do better removing the patch at bedtime.
Withdrawal can feel like anxiety (tight chest, edgy body, racing thoughts). NRT can lower that physiologic drive, but behavioral tools still matter for triggers.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to nicotine or any component of the formulation
OTC lozenge (self-care labeling): Do not use if allergic to soya (product dependent)

efficacy_response.patient_text: NRT doesn’t “treat anxiety” in the psychiatric sense—it treats nicotine withdrawal. When the withdrawal volume turns down, a lot of people feel calmer, less irritable, and less driven to smoke.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Patch provides slow, steady absorption; gum/lozenge absorb through the mouth; nasal spray absorbs through nasal mucosa
pharmacokinetics.onset: Nasal spray is fastest; gum/lozenge are next; patch is slowest but steady
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Nasal spray: ~10–20 minutes; inhalation: ≤15 minutes; gum: ~30 minutes; patch: ~2–8 hours
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Varies by formulation; nasal/inhaled forms are shorter; patch provides sustained delivery
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic (major), kidney and lung; many metabolites (including cotinine)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Acidic foods/beverages can decrease absorption of buccal nicotine (gum/lozenge)

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) helps you quit smoking by easing nicotine withdrawal symptoms—especially cravings, irritability, restlessness, and that wired, agitated feeling that can look like anxiety. It’s not a “mood med.” It’s a withdrawal tool that makes relapse less likely because you’re not white-knuckling it 24/7.
items: {link:condition:tobacco-use-disorder:Smoking cessation}: Helps reduce nicotine withdrawal symptoms (including craving) while you quit cigarettes
{link:condition:nicotine-withdrawal:Nicotine withdrawal relief}: Targets irritability, restlessness, agitation, sleep disruption, and concentration problems that spike right after quitting
Craving control strategy: Patch for steady baseline + gum/lozenge as “rescue” for breakthrough cravings (common and effective approach)
Extended support: Many people use NRT longer than 12 weeks to help prevent relapse, especially if cravings keep popping back up

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: NRT doesn’t feel like a “buzz” when it’s dosed right. It usually feels like withdrawal is quieter. Here’s what people commonly report:

quotes: It didn’t make me feel high. It made me feel less desperate.
The craving went from a 10 to like a 4. Still there, but manageable.
I could actually sit through a trigger without snapping.
I was still annoyed at everything… just not feral about it.
My brain stopped screaming for a cigarette every 20 minutes.
I felt more emotionally steady once withdrawal wasn’t driving me.
items.note: If you’re still super irritable, restless, or “can’t function,” that can be under-dosing, not personal failure. Dose can be adjusted (within limits).

items.category: Sleep and Dreams (especially with the patch)
quotes: The patch helped overnight cravings, but the dreams were… a lot.
I slept better once I stopped waking up in withdrawal at 3 a.m.
Taking the patch off at night fixed the weird dream stuff.
items.note: Some people do better wearing the patch 24 hours; others remove it at bedtime to avoid vivid dreams.

quotes: The gum burned a little at first, then I got used to it.
Lozenges made my throat feel peppery if I swallowed too much.
The nasal spray worked fast… and also made me sneeze like crazy.
items.note: These effects are common and usually improve. If you’re using it back-to-back nonstop, you’ll feel worse—pace it.

quotes: I got nauseated and shaky—turns out I was stacking products wrong.
My heart was racing and I felt sweaty. I backed off and it stopped.
I felt dizzy and gross—classic ‘too much nicotine’ signal.
items.note: Nausea, dizziness, sweating, weakness, fast heartbeat = your body asking for less nicotine (or asking you to stop smoking while on NRT).

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Different NRT forms hit at different speeds. Think: patch = steady background, gum/lozenge = faster “craving rescue,” nasal spray = fastest.
key_points: Nasal spray: fastest onset; reaches peak levels in ~10–20 minutes (most cigarette-like timing)
Gum/lozenge: typically noticeable within ~15–30 minutes; peak around ~30 minutes (varies by technique)
Patch: slow build; peak levels usually ~2–8 hours after applying a new patch
Patch duration: provides all-day nicotine delivery (16–24 hours depending on how you wear it)
Why this matters: if cravings spike fast, you often need a fast form (gum/lozenge) on top of a patch baseline

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: NRT works best when you treat it like a system: steady baseline nicotine (patch) plus targeted rescue doses (gum/lozenge) for triggers. The goal isn’t to feel “nothing.” The goal is to keep withdrawal quiet enough that your plan and skills can actually work.
sections.clinical_details: Many people relapse because withdrawal symptoms feel psychiatric—irritability, agitation, insomnia, restlessness, and concentration problems. NRT reduces that physiologic withdrawal drive so behavioral support (quit plan, trigger management, accountability) becomes doable instead of brutal.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Do not keep smoking while using NRT. Too much nicotine can make you seriously sick.
other: Cardiovascular risk: Nicotine can raise heart rate and blood pressure. Use caution if you have serious heart disease, recent heart attack, severe/worsening angina, significant arrhythmias, or uncontrolled hypertension.
Stop and get help if you have chest pain, severe palpitations, fainting, or signs of nicotine overdose (nausea/vomiting, dizziness, sweating, weakness, fast/irregular heartbeat).
GI disease: Use caution with active esophagitis or peptic ulcer disease (can worsen irritation).
Seizure history (OTC counseling): Some OTC labeling recommends medical advice before use if you have a history of seizures (product dependent).
Patch + MRI: Some patches may contain conducting metal; remove patch before MRI.
Do not use more than one patch at a time, and do not cut patches (can break delivery and irritate skin).
patient_counseling: Pick a quit date and stop smoking when you start NRT. The whole point is replacing cigarettes, not stacking nicotine on top of them.
If you feel nauseated, dizzy, sweaty, weak, or your heart is racing—back off. That’s nicotine overload.
Patch: rotate sites, don’t cut it, don’t wear more than one, and wash hands after handling.
Sleep: if vivid dreams or sleep disruption happens, remove the patch at bedtime and apply a new one in the morning.
Keep all nicotine products away from kids and pets. Nicotine can be toxic in small amounts.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Side effects are usually form-specific: mouth irritation with gum/lozenge, skin irritation with patch, nasal irritation with nasal spray. Overdoing nicotine can cause nausea, dizziness, sweating, and palpitations.
plain_language_list: Fast heartbeat or palpitations (especially if you’re getting too much nicotine)
Sleep disturbance or vivid dreams (patch, especially 24-hour wear)
Nasal irritation, sneezing, runny nose (nasal spray)

common.patient_note: A peppery or tingly sensation is expected. If you chew too fast or swallow too much nicotine, you may get hiccups, heartburn, or nausea. Slow down and use proper technique.
Can be nicotine withdrawal, nicotine itself, or both. If headaches worsen after dosing, consider nicotine overload or spacing doses out.

common.incidence: Common when dosing is too high or if you keep smoking
common.patient_note: This is your early warning system. Reduce dose, space doses, and confirm you’re not smoking on top of NRT.
Burning/irritation, sneezing, watery eyes, runny nose are extremely common early on and often improve with continued use.
If dreams get wild or sleep is worse, remove patch at bedtime and apply a new patch in the morning.
Rotate sites. Mild redness is common; if redness doesn’t resolve or you get significant rash/swelling, stop and contact a clinician.

serious: Severe nicotine toxicity: persistent vomiting, severe dizziness, confusion, weakness, cold sweat, fast/irregular pulse, fainting
Severe allergic reaction/anaphylaxis (rare): trouble breathing, swelling, widespread rash
Serious cardiac symptoms in high-risk patients: chest pain, dangerous arrhythmias (seek urgent care)

sections.heading: Critical Drug & Food Interactions
sections.intro: The biggest “interaction” in psychiatry isn’t nicotine itself—it’s what happens when you stop smoking. Cigarette smoke (not nicotine) induces CYP1A2. When you quit smoking, CYP1A2 activity can drop within about a week, and blood levels of some psychiatric meds can rise.

items.risk: When smoking stops, medication levels can rise significantly, increasing side effect/toxicity risk (sedation, dizziness, seizures for clozapine). NRT does NOT maintain the smoking-induced enzyme induction.
items.action: Tell your prescriber immediately if you’re quitting or cutting down. Plan for closer monitoring and possible dose adjustment. If you’re on clozapine, therapeutic drug monitoring is often needed.

items.with: Other CYP1A2-sensitive drugs (psychiatry-adjacent): caffeine, theophylline, some tricyclics (eg, imipramine), propranolol
items.risk: Quitting smoking can increase levels/effects of these substances, which can feel like anxiety, insomnia, tremor, or nausea (especially with caffeine).
items.action: As you quit, consider reducing caffeine and monitor for increased side effects from CYP1A2-metabolized medications.

items.risk: Acidic drinks/foods can reduce absorption of buccal nicotine, making it feel like the product “isn’t working.”
items.action: Avoid eating/drinking for 15 minutes before and while using gum/lozenge (especially coffee, soda, citrus).

items.risk: Nicotine overload (nausea, dizziness, sweating, palpitations), especially if stacking multiple NRT forms without a plan.
items.action: Quit smoking when you start NRT. If slips happen, don’t hide it—adjust the plan and get support.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: NRT isn’t a benzo taper situation—there’s no seizure-risk withdrawal from stopping NRT itself. The goal is to step down nicotine gradually so cravings don’t boomerang you back to cigarettes.
key_points: Patch: step down dose over weeks (eg, 21 → 14 → 7 mg) rather than stopping abruptly if cravings are still strong.
Gum/lozenge: taper by stretching time between doses and reducing total daily pieces/lozenges over time.
Nasal spray: typically tapered over weeks (do not exceed recommended max use duration).
Extended duration (>12 weeks) is common in real life when relapse risk is high—especially if cravings keep coming back.
If you’re still craving hard at the planned stop date, that’s a signal to adjust the plan, not “just power through.”

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Dosing depends on the form. Patch is your steady baseline. Gum/lozenge are fast “rescue” for cravings. The #1 rule is to stop smoking when you start, and dose consistently enough early on (under-dosing is one of the biggest reasons people think NRT “doesn’t work”).

adult.gum_strength_selection: If you smoke your first cigarette within 30 minutes of waking, use 4 mg gum; otherwise 2 mg gum is recommended.
adult.gum_weeks_1_6: Chew 1 piece every 1 to 2 hours; maximum 24 pieces/day. To increase quit success, chew at least 9 pieces/day during the first 6 weeks.
adult.gum_weeks_7_9: Chew 1 piece every 2 to 4 hours; maximum 24 pieces/day.
adult.gum_weeks_10_12: Chew 1 piece every 4 to 8 hours; maximum 24 pieces/day.
adult.gum_breakthrough_cravings: If strong or frequent cravings persist after 1 piece, you may use a second piece within the hour. Do not continuously use one piece right after another.
adult.lozenge_strength_selection: If you smoke your first cigarette within 30 minutes of waking, use 4 mg lozenge; otherwise 2 mg lozenge is recommended.
adult.lozenge_weeks_1_6: Use 1 lozenge every 1 to 2 hours; maximum 20 lozenges/day (and do not exceed 5 lozenges per 6 hours). To increase quit success, use at least 9 lozenges/day during the first 6 weeks.
adult.lozenge_weeks_7_9: Use 1 lozenge every 2 to 4 hours; maximum 20 lozenges/day (and do not exceed 5 lozenges per 6 hours).
adult.lozenge_weeks_10_12: Use 1 lozenge every 4 to 8 hours; maximum 20 lozenges/day (and do not exceed 5 lozenges per 6 hours).
adult.patch_>10_cigarettes_per_day: Step 1: 21 mg/day for 6 weeks, then Step 2: 14 mg/day for 2 weeks, then Step 3: 7 mg/day for 2 weeks.
adult.patch_≤10_cigarettes_per_day: Step 2: 14 mg/day for 6 weeks, then Step 3: 7 mg/day for 2 weeks.
adult.patch_adjustment_tip: If you have withdrawal symptoms/cravings, a higher step may be needed; if side effects occur (nausea, palpitations, dizziness), step down or reassess dosing strategy.
adult.nasal_spray_initial: Use 1 to 2 doses per hour as needed (each dose = 2 sprays, one in each nostril, delivering 1 mg nicotine per dose).
adult.nasal_spray_max: Do not exceed 5 doses/hour (10 sprays/hour) or 40 doses/day (80 sprays/day = 40 mg/day). Do not use longer than 3 months unless directed; use beyond 6 months is not recommended.
adult.nasal_spray_minimum_effective: For best results, use at least 8 doses/day; using less is unlikely to be effective.
adult.nasal_spray_if_not_quit_by_week_4: If unable to stop smoking by the fourth week, consider discontinuation and reassessment of treatment strategy.
adult.inhaler_us_availability: Nicotrol Inhaler is no longer available in the United States.

sections.simple_explanation: Patch = steady background nicotine to prevent all-day withdrawal. Gum/lozenge = faster relief for cravings and triggers. Nasal spray (Rx) = fastest onset and can feel closest to cigarette timing, but commonly irritates the nose/throat.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Nicotine exposure isn’t “free,” but cigarette smoke is far worse than nicotine alone. In pregnancy and breastfeeding, decisions are about harm reduction and supervision. In kidney/liver disease, nicotine clearance can be reduced—meaning the same dose can hit harder.
sections.pregnancy: Nicotine crosses the placenta. Behavioral support is first-line in pregnancy. Evidence for medication in pregnancy is more limited and mixed; if NRT is used, it should be under close medical supervision and with a clear commitment to quit smoking. Pregnancy can increase nicotine clearance, so withdrawal may still break through—this requires clinician-guided adjustment rather than self-escalation.
sections.lactation: Nicotine and cotinine can appear in breast milk. Breastfeeding is still generally recommended over formula even if a parent smokes, but reducing/stopping nicotine exposure is ideal. NRT may reduce the infant’s exposure to secondhand smoke compared to continued smoking. If using short-acting NRT (gum/lozenge), avoid dosing immediately before breastfeeding to create a longer nicotine-free interval. Individualize decisions with shared decision-making.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing. Older adults may be more sensitive to nicotine effects like palpitations and sleep disruption; start with the lowest effective approach and monitor closely, especially if cardiovascular disease is present.
sections.hepatic: No specific manufacturer dose adjustments are provided, but nicotine clearance can be decreased in moderate to severe hepatic impairment. Use caution, monitor for adverse effects (nausea, dizziness, palpitations), and consider dose reduction if needed.
sections.renal: No specific manufacturer dose adjustments are provided, but nicotine clearance can be decreased in moderate to severe renal impairment. Use caution, monitor for adverse effects, and consider dose reduction if needed.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Smoking status and relapse risk: confirm complete smoking cessation (or slips) and adjust the plan rather than pretending slips didn’t happen.
Withdrawal symptom control (psychiatry-relevant): cravings, irritability, agitation, restlessness, anxiety-like symptoms, sleep disruption, concentration problems.
Nicotine toxicity symptoms: severe headache, dizziness, confusion, disturbed vision/hearing, abdominal pain; rapid/weak/irregular pulse; salivation, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cold sweat, weakness.
Cardiovascular symptoms (especially in high-risk patients): chest pain, palpitations, irregular heartbeat, elevated blood pressure.
Sleep and dreams (patch): insomnia, vivid dreams, nighttime awakenings; adjust patch wear time if needed.
Skin reactions (patch): persistent redness, rash, blistering; rotate sites and discontinue if severe or persistent.

Drug level/side-effect changes after quitting smoking (CYP1A2 shift): watch closely if patient uses clozapine/olanzapine or other CYP1A2-sensitive meds; consider therapeutic drug monitoring when indicated.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: NRT comes in multiple forms so you can match speed and coverage to your cravings. Many people do best with a patch baseline plus a fast form for triggers.
items: Transdermal patch (OTC): 7 mg/24 hr, 14 mg/24 hr, 21 mg/24 hr
Nicotine gum (OTC, nicotine polacrilex): 2 mg and 4 mg
Nicotine lozenge/mini lozenge (OTC, nicotine polacrilex): 2 mg and 4 mg
Nicotrol Inhaler: Not available in the United States (discontinued)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Nicotine binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the brain and body. In the brain, it drives stimulation and reward signaling—part of why cigarettes are so reinforcing. NRT gives controlled nicotine levels to reduce withdrawal and cravings while you break the behavioral loop of smoking.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: For tobacco use disorder, NRT is a frontline medication option—especially when withdrawal symptoms look and feel psychiatric (agitation, insomnia, irritability, restlessness, anxious body). Patch + a short-acting form (gum/lozenge) is a common, practical approach. Nasal spray can be useful when cravings hit fast and hard, but irritation limits tolerability. The best outcomes come from combining NRT with behavioral support (skills + plan + accountability).

seo.title: Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT): Patch, Gum, Lozenge & Nasal Spray for Quitting Smoking
seo.description: Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) helps you quit smoking by reducing withdrawal (cravings, irritability, agitation, sleep disruption). Patch dosing steps, gum/lozenge 12-week schedule, nasal spray dosing, side effects, interactions with psych meds after quitting smoking, and safe step-down.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: What is nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) used for?
faqs.a: NRT is used to help you quit smoking by relieving nicotine withdrawal symptoms—especially cravings, irritability, restlessness, and agitation. It gives your brain controlled nicotine without the toxic cocktail of cigarette smoke.

Not in the usual sense. NRT doesn’t treat an anxiety disorder or depression. It treats nicotine withdrawal, which can look psychiatric (edgy body, irritability, insomnia, agitation). When withdrawal calms down, people often feel more emotionally steady.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between the patch and gum/lozenge?
faqs.a: The patch is steady baseline coverage (all-day). Gum and lozenges are faster acting and work best as “rescue” for cravings and triggers. A common strategy is patch + gum/lozenge, because cravings don’t always follow a schedule.

faqs.q: How do I choose 2 mg vs 4 mg gum or lozenge?
faqs.a: A simple rule: if you smoke your first cigarette within 30 minutes of waking, 4 mg is usually recommended. If you wait longer than 30 minutes, 2 mg is typically recommended.

faqs.q: Can I smoke while using NRT?
faqs.a: You shouldn’t. Smoking on top of NRT increases your risk of nicotine overdose—nausea, dizziness, sweating, weakness, and fast/irregular heartbeat. If you slip and smoke, don’t hide it—adjust the plan and get support.

faqs.q: What are signs I’m getting too much nicotine?
faqs.a: Classic nicotine overload symptoms include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, sweating, weakness, headache, and a rapid or irregular heartbeat. If this happens, reduce dosing, space doses out, and make sure you’re not smoking while on NRT.

faqs.q: Why does quitting smoking matter for psychiatric meds like clozapine or olanzapine?
faqs.a: Cigarette smoke (not nicotine) induces CYP1A2. When you stop smoking, CYP1A2 activity can drop within about a week, and levels of meds like clozapine and olanzapine can rise—sometimes a lot. NRT does NOT keep that enzyme induction going. If you’re quitting or cutting down, tell your prescriber so monitoring and dose adjustments can happen safely.

faqs.q: Does the nicotine patch cause vivid dreams?
faqs.a: It can. If vivid dreams or sleep disruption is a problem, many people do better removing the patch at bedtime and applying a new patch in the morning. If nighttime cravings wake you up, 24-hour wear may help—this is a tradeoff you can personalize.

faqs.q: How long should I use NRT?
faqs.a: Many plans are 8–12 weeks, but longer use is common if relapse risk is high or cravings persist. The goal is staying off cigarettes; stepping down more slowly is often better than stopping early and rebounding back to smoking.

faqs.q: Is NRT safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: These are individualized decisions. Behavioral support is first-line in pregnancy. If NRT is used during pregnancy, it should be under medical supervision and with a clear commitment to quit smoking. In breastfeeding, nicotine can pass into milk, but NRT may still reduce infant harm compared with continued smoking—shared decision-making matters here.

faqs.q: What’s the fastest form of NRT?
faqs.a: Nicotine nasal spray (prescription) is the fastest and can feel closest to cigarette timing. Gum/lozenge are next. The patch is slowest to build but gives steady all-day coverage.
